item.title: Bridging digitalisation, sustainability, and resilience through systems thinking tools: Integrated perspectives and collaborative practices for SMEs
item.content:encoded:
Rui Torres de Oliveira, Deakin University

Agnes Toth-Peter, University of Queensland

Martie-Louise Verreynne, University of Queensland

David Audretsch, Indiana University

Domenico Dentoni, MBS School of Business

Andrea Chiarini, University of Verona

The 21st century presents a range of complex and interdependent challenges, including climate change, resource depletion, economic inequality, and technological disruptions. These so-called wicked problems demand a paradigm shift in our approach to problem-solving. Addressing such challenges requires multi-stakeholder partnerships and holistic, systems-level approaches that transcend traditional, siloed methodologies. Systems thinking, a powerful tool for understanding complexity and interconnections, offers a pathway to sustainable solutions.

Although systems theory became foundational in fields such as environmental sciences during the 20th century, its adoption in strategic management research has been more limited. This reluctance may be tied to the enduring influence of reductionist approaches rooted in early scientific management and innovation models. A systems perspective is critical as it views organizations as complex adaptive systems or 'functioning wholes', which contrasts with problem-solving focusing on isolated components. This special collection aims to bring systems thinking methodologies to the forefront and inspire a deeper engagement with systems-based frameworks and tools, advancing both theoretical and practical understanding of their application in business and management contexts, as well as their transformative potential in addressing complex, interconnected challenges.

By shifting away from traditional reductionist approaches, we seek to highlight how systems thinking can uncover hidden dynamics, identify leverage points, and foster innovative solutions at the intersection of sustainability and digitalization. The new technologies of the Industry 4.0 revolution, including data-driven insights, automation and increased transparency, are changing the way businesses operate. However, it is important to better understand the impact of these disruptive innovations as a result of rapidly progressing digital technologies, as they often convey a dark side of digital change in the social and environmental context. This duality highlights the importance of applying systems thinking to ensure that digital transformation aligns with sustainability goals. Within the sustainability domain, the circular economy introduces a new economic system and logic that also fundamentally disrupts business-as-usual. This requires a shift from individual-level innovation to collective solutions, thus relying on an ecosystem and systemic approaches to achieve a whole-of-lifecycle perspective and integrate supply chains to create closed-loop systems. However, existing tools and frameworks often fail to accommodate the complexity of such an interconnected approach, limiting their effectiveness in addressing the challenges of circularity and disruptive digital solutions.

Recent literature increasingly calls for holistic, systems-level assessments and methodologies to address complex sustainability challenges. While 'system change' and 'systems thinking' often appear in the political, industry and academic discourse, these calls have yet to be fully realized. Nonetheless, the superficial adoption of systems thinking, which neglects the tools and methods to uncover underlying feedback mechanisms and behaviour over time, risks creating a façade of systemic awareness while inadvertently exacerbating issues and rebound effects, ultimately worsening the planetary crisis. This online collection seeks to bridge this gap by highlighting innovative research and practices and by advancing our understanding of interconnected systems and the leverage points within them, we can develop more effective business strategies for achieving resilience and sustainable development.

In this call for papers, we emphasize the importance of 'real' systemic change in the contexts of sustainability, digitalization, and resilience. By aspiring to a real system change, we recognize that defining what constitutes a 'real' systemic shift remains a challenging, often contested but also underdeveloped issue, with scholars often using terms such as 'systemic change', 'system change' or 'transformative change', or using 'systems thinking' without the adequate tools and methodologies applied. There is also a variety among the types of systems across disciplines, definitions used and their scale, which makes this even more difficult to clarify. The literature points to examples, such as large-scale system changes that involve both the breadth of engaging large numbers of people, institutions, and geographies, as well as the depth of transforming the complex power structures and relationships within these systems. Cross-sector partnerships navigating wicked problems are often marked by knowledge uncertainty, value conflicts, and complexity, which require adaptable governance processes to continuously reassess the problem over time. Addressing a complex issue often requires assessing the levers and solutions by examining cross-boundary impacts across different systems and sectors. Expanding the boundary can offer additional insights into intervention points, revealing hidden mechanisms or suggesting that the most effective leverage may lie on someone else's patch. Thus, there is a need for new studies and frameworks that capture the complex interactions between actors, partnerships, and societal issues, across different levels, metrics and scales. Together, these perspectives illustrate that 'real' systemic change is not a static, singular transformation, but an evolving process shaped by diverse and often conflicting stakeholder interests, involving cross-boundary and cross-sector connections.

We invite contributions that explore and contribute to the better understanding of 'real' systemic change, through investigating the synergy between systems thinking, sustainability, and digitalisation. Accordingly, this online collection aims to address the urgent need for a paradigm shift in how we conceptualise and tackle grand challenges, building upon cross-sector partnerships and value co-creation, leveraging frameworks like the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), circular economy principles, and the transformative potential of Industry 4.0 and 5.0 technologies. We invite contributors to discover and use a wide range of tools within systems thinking, including but not limited to causal loop diagrams, system archetypes, system maps, system dynamics models, group model building, and participatory methods.

Potential topics

  • Applications of systems thinking tools, such as causal loop diagrams (CLDs), system archetypes, and system dynamics modeling, in addressing sustainability challenges
  • Development and validation of systems-level frameworks and methodologies for sustainable development
  • Case studies demonstrating the impact of systems thinking on real-world sustainability and/or digitalisation initiatives
  • Use of group model building and participatory system dynamics to support interdisciplinary and ecosystem solutions
  • Exploration of system archetypes and system dynamics models to identify leverage points for driving transformational change and to investigate levers in cross-boundary settings
  • The role of digital technologies, including IoT, AI, big data, and blockchain, in enabling systems-level insights and solutions in the circular economy and sustainability initiatives
  • Integration of digitalisation with circular economy strategies and Industry 5.0 principles and potentials
  • Innovative approaches to digital transformation that promote sustainable development
  • Cross-sectoral and interdisciplinary research to foster collaboration in bridging sustainability and digitalisation, using systems thinking
  • The role of ecosystems in sustainable business models and the boundaries of entrepreneurial ecosystems
  • Methodologies for recognising, assessing and addressing the interconnectedness of environmental, economic, and social systems
  • Open innovation in new sustainable businesses, considering distinct institutional contexts and economic systems, such as emerging and developed economies

  • May 31, 2027: Manuscript deadline for rolling submissions

item.title: Organizing Sustainably with Nature in the Global South
item.content:encoded:
Simone Barakat, Fundação Getulio Vargas

Maria Ehrnström-Fuentes, Hanken School of Economics

Seray Ergene, University of Rhode Island

Steffen Farny, Leuphana University Luneburg

Judy Muthuri, University of the West Indies

Contemporary sustainability challenges increasingly foreground organizations as embedded within complex social-ecological systems rather than operating independently from them. While ecological degradation and resource constraints affect organizations worldwide, these challenges are more immediate and structurally embedded in the operating environments of the Global South. These challenges are not just a background context to which organizations must adapt but an outcome of long-standing patterns of extraction, uneven development, and entrenched social inequalities that continue to shape what sustainability can mean in practice.

Although sustainability has gained prominence in Management and Organization Studies in recent years, the field continues to draw predominantly on Global North epistemologies, experiences, and assumptions. While important exceptions engage with ecocentric, posthumanist, and indigenous approaches to organizing, sustainability research in MOS remains overwhelmingly theorized from Global North contexts, leaving many southern voices and experiences marginalized. This marginalization does not imply an absence of sustainability-oriented organizing in the Global South. On the contrary, a growing body of work examines organizing in the Global South in ways that directly address issues such as environmental degradation, community resilience, and socio-ecological justice. However, much of this work is not explicitly framed as "sustainability" research and therefore remains peripheral to mainstream MOS debates. Consequently, despite rich empirical insights, we still lack a robust understanding of how organizations in the Global South pursue sustainability under conditions of severe climate vulnerabilities and entrenched power asymmetries.

Recent developments in sustainability scholarship have brought to the fore regenerative forms of organizing that recognize the interdependence among economic activity and ecological integrity. This scholarship emphasizes place-based practices that work with nature and that cultivate resilience and long-term ecological viability. Such forms of organizing have long existed in the Global South, grounded in relational understandings of land, community, and more-than-human worlds. This marginalization of southern voices raises ethical questions about who gets to define what is considered 'sustainable' and how the dominance of northern perspectives not only marginalizes stakeholders and their visions but also determines who benefits from how this concept is defined.

Engaging with sustainability practices and knowledges from the Global South provides an urgently needed ground for expanding and challenging the conceptual foundations of how sustainability is theorized and made sense of in organizational contexts that are marked by contradictions and vulnerabilities that are often not visible in (but also part of) the Global North. A better understanding of southern perspectives on sustainability can fundamentally expand existing theories and thus shape MOS research and debates beyond the Global South.

This Special Issue responds to the dearth in the literature by inviting both theoretical and empirical submissions on how sustainability is organized and defined in the Global South. The Special Issue broadly understands Global South as both an empirical location which is "apart and distinct from North America and Europe [and Australia]" and as a "challenge to universalist knowledge" where scholars reformulate concepts around sustainability based on empirical accounts and voices from the Global South. The Global North and Global South are not separated by a strict boundary; rather, these organizational contexts are marked by friction and interdependence. This allows research to focus on and articulate sustainability definitions and organizing processes that are upheld by North-South relations, such as global supply chains or environmental governance.

The Special Issue is particularly interested in work that considers the embeddedness of organizations within social–ecological systems and that engages sustainability not as a generic concern, but as a core organizing challenge shaped by place and history. The Special Issue aims to advance a pluralistic perspective from multiple contexts, theories, and concepts instead of a unifying theory for all communities on all continents. Submissions may draw on diverse theoretical traditions and methodological approaches, including those grounded in indigenous, decolonial, relational, posthumanist, or other traditional ecological knowledge pertinent to the Global South, and may focus on organizations of various forms, including firms, cooperatives, social enterprises, community organizations, and hybrid arrangements.

In sum, this Special Issue aims to generate organizational knowledge that is both theoretically generative and practically relevant for organizing sustainability in a world of multiple crises.

Potential topics

  • Organizing for Environmental Sustainability across Communities and Regions - How do communities and organizations work together to govern natural resources and shared ecological commons?
  • How do sustainability standards, certifications, and supply-chain rules influence organizational practices across regions?
  • How do organizations manage environmental interdependencies across local and global contexts?
  • What challenges arise when local ecological priorities clash with global market or regulatory pressures, and how do organizations deal with these challenges in practice?
  • Organizing with Nature from a Global South perspective - How do organizations in the Global South manage their activities within the carrying ecological capacity of the planet (i.e., planetary boundaries), particularly under conditions of resource constraints and institutional fragility?
  • How do organizations in the Global South engage with degrowth, sufficiency, circular, or regenerative practices?
  • What tensions do organizations in the Global South face between economic survival and ecological realities, and how do they navigate these circumstances in practice?
  • How organizations in the Global South conceptualize and manage their embeddedness within social–ecological systems and attempt to develop a regenerative dynamic with nature?
  • Power, Inequality, and the Governance of Nature - What are the sources of environmental injustices currently in the global South? How are they experienced? What are some resistances to these injustices, and how do they unfold? What are some policy mechanisms (if any) to address these injustices?
  • How do power asymmetries manifest in sustainability governance and transnational regulations?
  • How do corporations influence environmental policy and access to natural resources?
  • How do resistance and counter-organizing emerge around contested environmental futures?
  • Stakeholders and Environmental Sustainability from a Global South Perspective - How do organizations in the Global South engage with stakeholders in relation to environmental sustainability?
  • How are the interests of diverse stakeholders, such as communities, governments, NGOs, and other stakeholders, navigated around environmental risks and resource use?
  • How do stakeholder relationships influence organizational decisions and practices related to environmental sustainability?
  • How do power asymmetries and dependency relations among stakeholders shape environmental outcomes and organizing processes?

item.title: Collective actorhood and organizationality: Recalibrating responsibility in business-society relations
item.content:encoded:
Dennis Schoeneborn, Copenhagen Business School

Héloïse Berkowitz, CNRS, Aix Marseille University

Leonhard Dobusch, University of Innsbruck

Frank de Bakker, IÉSEG School of Management

Consuelo Vásquez, Université du Québec à Montréal (UQAM)

Over the past decades, the relations between business and society have fundamentally changed. We are entering an age of digital futures with artificial intelligence taking over more and more human tasks at rapid speed, as well as broken futures with accelerating dynamics of climate change, in which the survival of humankind will depend on our ability to organize in collective ways and imagine alternatives to tackle such complex social problems, amidst growing inequalities and ecological destruction on a planetary scale.

Collective actorhood, defined as the capacity of a social group to act on a supra-individual level and to become considered as an agent in its own right, has been argued to be the main criterion that distinguishes organizations from other social phenomena. However, the current crisis of civilization—a crisis of climate, energy, poverty, inequality, food, and meaning—can only be addressed if we consider that collective actorhood often requires to reach beyond the boundaries of single organizations and involve a much broader spectrum of organizational phenomena. Examples like cross-sector partnerships, meta-organizations, or open organizing phenomena that resemble social movements all tend to have in common that their status as collective actor is far less clear-cut or that collective agency may be accomplished in different ways.

For studying such recalibrations of business-society relations, organization and management scholarship has started to draw on gradual understandings of organization. Prominent examples of this view are the notions of partial organization or organizationality. These gradual theories of organization hold much promise for rethinking collective actorhood beyond the boundaries of formal organizations. Similarly, indigenous, feminist, and decolonial approaches further invite us to question the Global North's conceptualizations of organizations and to consider also how organizing happens at the margins. Most research on organizationality takes the starting point in situations of privilege where actors deliberately choose to organize themselves in loose and fluid ways. Adopting alternative ontologies invites a better account for situations in which marginalized actors are forced into fluid and precarious ways of organizing.

If we relate gradual understandings of organization to matters of collective actorhood, we can observe that actorhood can vary by degree, as well. Corporations increasingly portray themselves as collective actors in their own right, for instance, by positioning themselves as corporate citizens, thus strongly emphasizing their responsibility as collective actors vis-à-vis society. However, the question arises whether trends of an over-organization of the business-society relations fosters or rather dilutes the responsibility of the collective actors involved. On the other hand, we see trends of less pronounced collective actorhood. Digital platform organizations have been shown to strategically downplay their status as collective actors to diminish their collective responsibility for the malicious content that is shared on their platforms, while profiteering from such sharing at the same time. Furthermore, multinational corporations strategize to escape actorhood and avoid taking responsibility for the destruction of people and nature.

This Special Issue invites scholarship to further explore both these empirical trends and the new theoretical approaches that shed a different light on the changing relations between business and society with regard to more or less pronounced forms of collective actorhood. We are interested in strategic as well as emergent processes that allow for different degrees of collective actorhood over time and the respective implications for business-society relations. We also encourage critical reflections on the very notion of collective actorhood, along with alternative conceptualizations that may deepen our understanding of how organizations can be made more responsive and accountable in the face of contemporary societal crises. We invite conceptual and empirical inquiries into the dynamics of collective actorhood from a broad variety of theoretical perspectives, including gradual understandings of organization, as well as a broad set of methodological approaches.

Potential topics

  • How is collective actorhood performed and organized?
  • Is a legal status/legal person needed to accomplish collective actorhood?
  • Why and how do actors strategically downplay or amplify collective actorhood? How do these strategic efforts affect responsibility attributions?
  • What are the implications and limitations of collective actorhood for reenvisioning the business-society relationship and offer alternative solutions in crises of civilization?
  • Where and how does actorhood emerge? How do institutional contexts affect actorhood?
  • How does actorhood evolve over time or space, and how do organizations transition between different degrees of organizationality?
  • Can social collectives be perpetuated and maintained even with a low degree of organizationality – or do they feel pressures either to be dissolved or evolve toward higher degrees of organizationality eventually?
  • How to explain asymmetric dynamics between the organized (e.g., established formal organizations; high degree of organizationality) and the (rather) unorganized as their counterparts (e.g., social media firestorm; low degree of organizationality)?
  • What can we learn from alternative forms of organizing, including those in marginalized settings?
  • How is collective actorhood conceptualized in the various geographies, including the Global South? How does this translate, circulate, and adapt across geographies?
  • What are the contributions of other collective notions stemming from indigenous cosmovisions and decolonial approaches?
  • How does actorhood affect the interactions between organizations from different domains (for profit and non-profit, scientific organizations, public actors, etc.)?
  • When does collective actorhood create relations of domination and exploitation?
  • At what point does collective actorhood become constitutive of societal problems and crises (incl. fascism, techno-feudalism, etc.) – rather than a solution for addressing them?
  • How does actorhood (or the lack of) affect the relationship between privileged and marginal communities?
  • Can living (forests, rivers, soils) and non-living (algorithms, technologies) entities be attributed actorhood and be held accountable? How does it differ from 'human' organizing?
  • How can alternative ontologies help inform this analysis?
  • How can a gradual understanding of organization help us to understand variations in the degree of organizational actorhood and responsibility attributions in the relations between businesses and society?
  • What are the parameters of organizationality required for a responsible collective actorhood?
  • How can alternative ontologies, cosmovisions, and organizing experiences inform this critical reflection?
  • How to better account for situations in which marginalized actors are forced into fluid and precarious ways of organizing and/or have no choice to lessen the degree of organizationality to cope or survive?

item.title: Organizing within the Planetary Boundaries
item.content:encoded:
Steve Kennedy, Rotterdam School of Management, Erasmus University

Brooke Lahneman, Montana State University

Lucrezia Nava, University of Exeter Business School

Amanda Williams, EM Lyon Business School

Scholarship on business sustainability increasingly views organizations as embedded within natural systems, conceptualized through the planetary boundaries framework. The planetary boundary framework defines nine Earth system processes that regulate the planet's stability and resilience and are directly affected by human activity. Alarmingly, seven of these nine boundaries have now been crossed, threatening both natural systems and the economies that depend on them. For business scholarship, this creates an urgent need to understand how organizations can operate and manage within the safe space delineated by planetary boundaries.

Much prior research on the natural environment in management has privileged firm-level outcomes such as financial performance and has overlooked the complex, coupled dynamics of ecological, social, and organizational systems. Drawing from ecology and biophysical system science, the planetary boundary framework provides both the conceptual and empirical depth to address this complexity and a scientifically grounded map of global limits to study how organizations affect — and are affected by — key ecological processes. It also serves as a boundary tool that enables interdisciplinary collaboration between management scholars and natural scientists.

Business scholars and practitioners increasingly recognize the need for deeper insight into sustainability that treats natural systems as operational and strategic constraints, as seen in rising attention to practical efforts such as the Science Based Targets Initiative to help companies align with planetary boundaries. However, integrating the planetary boundary framework into organizational research remains a challenge. One reason is that management research has largely been grounded in organization-focused theories and social science methodologies, with limited engagement with the natural sciences as a conceptual or empirical foundation. As a result, despite a growing body of work, a cohesive understanding of how the planetary boundary framework can bring the biophysical to the fore in organizational scholarship is still lacking.

This Special Issue responds to this gap by advancing the integration of the planetary boundary framework into management research and accelerating actionable insights into how organizations, their leaders, and the communities they affect can operate within planetary boundaries. The central question is: How can the planetary boundary framework be leveraged to develop theory and practice that illuminate the embeddedness of organizations within natural systems? Contributions should move beyond treating the natural environment as mere context, to position planetary boundaries as core organizing principles for theorizing, measuring, and guiding organizational action.

The Special Issue aims to spark scholarship that develops new concepts and empirical evidence grounded in biophysical system science; examines how organizations, industries, governments, and communities contribute to, or help avert, planetary boundary transgressions; and explores governance and innovation pathways that enable organizations to thrive while remaining within a safe and just operating space. The special issue sets out to push other boundaries too: the combined interdisciplinary networks of the guest editors allow drawing on natural scientists as readers, contributors, and reviewers to ensure reliable scientific evidence.

Both theoretical and empirical submissions from across business sustainability research are invited, with particular interest in studies that examine how organizations engage with biophysical limits and operate within the safe space defined by the planetary boundaries framework, leveraging planetary boundary concepts, models, or data to inform strategy, decision-making, and policy engagement. Studies investigating how organizations develop proactive and responsive strategies to address the interconnections between planetary boundaries and social issues, and studies that synthesize empirical insights from organizations and engage in forward-looking theorizing about how the planetary boundary framework could reshape organizing are welcome.

Research that emerges from collaboration with natural scientists or applies natural science methods and measures such as geospatial data, biodiversity and genetic diversity indicators is especially encouraged. While management research has focused heavily on climate change, papers addressing the other eight planetary boundaries are particularly welcome, including biosphere integrity, freshwater change, land-system change, biogeochemical flows, ocean acidification, stratospheric ozone depletion, atmospheric aerosol loading, and novel entities.

Potential topics

  • How Organizations Integrate the Planetary Boundary Framework into Strategy and Action
  • How organizations leverage planetary boundaries to inform sustainability materiality assessments and sustainability strategies
  • How organizations collectively use planetary boundaries as a basis to inform shared understanding of cross-scale risks across space and time
  • How organizations leverage planetary boundaries to inform risk management approaches
  • How organizations collectively build adaptive capacity for addressing risks and identifying opportunities associated with the planetary boundary framework
  • How organizations utilize planetary boundaries to inform creation of sustainability targets such as SBTi and corporate reporting on environmental impacts
  • How organizations disaggregate planetary boundaries to relevant temporal and spatial scales to inform appropriate action for sustainability
  • How organizations use the planetary boundary framework to shape sectoral and cross-sector collaborations
  • How organizations leverage planetary boundaries as a way to 'unlock' the complexity of the natural environment for business model innovation and/or product design
  • How Organizations Can Operate and Manage within Individual Planetary Boundaries
  • How organizations detect, interpret, and act when a planetary boundary is being approached or transgressed
  • How organizations prepare for risks associated with transgressing the boundaries and innovate to limit planetary boundary transgression
  • How organizations use planetary boundaries for constraint-driven innovation for enhanced practices, processes, business models, and/or collaborations
  • Which processes and practices enable firms to develop proactive and responsive strategies for long-term engagement with a specific planetary boundary
  • How organizations should balance trade-offs between proactive and responsive strategies for a given planetary boundary, given their industry and operating context
  • What roles different stakeholders play in shaping organizational responses to planetary boundary transgressions
  • How organizations can engage with least-studied boundaries such as ocean acidification, biogeochemical flows, atmospheric aerosol loading, stratospheric ozone depletion, and novel entities
  • How to Navigate Interconnections among Planetary Boundaries and with Social Foundations
  • How organizations adapt and innovate strategies, practices, and processes to address interconnections among multiple planetary boundaries
  • How efforts to stay within planetary boundaries can be aligned with advancing key social foundations and UN Sustainable Development Goals
  • How organizations can apply systems-thinking lenses to manage non-linear change, ecosystem risks, and feedback loops across planetary boundaries and/or social systems
  • What governance mechanisms, decision tools, or collaborative arrangements enable organizations and industries to navigate and manage trade-offs across boundaries
  • What role could concepts such as degrowth, carrying capacity, or post-growth business models play in helping organizations remain within interconnected ecological limits
  • How to Develop Alternative Organizational Theories and Practices from Planetary Boundary Biophysical Foundations
  • What innovations in practices, products, and business models emerge when organizational thinking begins with planetary boundaries
  • How integrating the planetary boundary framework can inform or reshape core organizational theories
  • How the planetary boundary framework can inform theory on crisis management and responding to ecosystem shocks such as natural disasters
  • How the planetary boundary framework might advance perspectives on desirable or alternative futures
  • What alternative forms of organizing can be theorized by taking planetary boundaries as foundational
  • How theory on circular and regenerative systems can be informed by considering planetary boundaries

Timeline

  • March 1, 2027: Full manuscript submission deadline

item.title: Imagining Post-Growth
item.content:encoded:
Fred Basso, London School of Economics and Political Science

Nil Özçağlar-Toulouse, Université de Lille

Julien Troiville, ESG Université du Québec À Montréal

Humanity has entered a critical period to limit catastrophic climate change. Global warming is primarily due to human activity, and efforts to remain below 1.5°C have been insufficient. More than ever, marketing must act to encourage behaviors and choices compatible with truly sustainable lifestyles. Post-growth has emerged as a major research topic, carried by environmental and economic sciences as well as social sciences such as history, sociology and political science. It challenges the dependence of our societies on economic growth, the central place accorded to consumption-based well-being, and the supposed link between prosperity and productivism.

Interest in post-growth is reflected in the proliferation of articles in renowned scientific journals, the release of documentaries, and the creation of research centers dedicated to this topic. Management sciences are also engaged, as evidenced by calls for contributions for special issues devoted to post-growth or edited works. This special issue aims to advance theory and practice by exploring how researchers, consumers and practitioners implement strategies to prepare for post-growth.

This special issue welcomes empirical and conceptual contributions addressing post-growth in marketing from various theoretical, methodological and disciplinary angles (economics, psychology, history, law...), as well as research in non-WEIRD contexts and with indigenous and decolonial perspectives. In accordance with the principles of 'sobriety in research' and open science, particular attention will be given to proposals based on open data, panel data, and similar sources. In spring, a writing workshop in format will be organized and details will be communicated through various channels.

Potential topics

  • How marketing can challenge the status quo: Creating new desires vs. responding to individual needs; Marketing as a political choice reinforcing capitalism; Critical reflection on critical marketing; Ethical marketing practices and their relationship to the economic system; Individual vs. systemic responsibility in consumer behavior (I-frame vs. S-frame); Nudging and boosting as neoliberal strategies
  • How marketing can engage in degrowth practices: Transformative practices for degrowth strategies; Role of marketing experts in post-growth economic transitions; Reinventing marketing practices, training and education; Overcoming tensions within the economy; Internal growth transformations and moving away from materialism; Conceptual clarification of degrowth, post-growth, demarketing, regenerative economy, donut economy, ecosocial marketing, decarbonized marketing
  • How a post-growth economy can be sustained: Transitioning from unlimited desires to meeting human needs; Consumption corridors and sufficient consumption; Marketing roles and practices to maintain in post-growth society; Reduced working time and prefigurative organizations; Moving beyond technological utopias to social utopias; Public policies for degrowth transitions; Economic development equity between Global North and South; Escaping extractivism and postcolonial systems

item.title: SMEs: Towards New Business Models?
item.content:encoded:
Marion Polge, Université de Montpellier

Isabelle Calmé, Université de Tours

Colette Fourcade, Université de Montpellier

For a long time considered as the "small scale" of SMEs, Very Small Enterprises (SMEs) remain marginalized as an autonomous object of study in management research. Yet the foundational work of P.-A. Julien and M. Marchesnay laid essential foundations: the first by highlighting the constitutive heterogeneity of the SME population, the second by identifying the characteristics specific to the management system of the "hypofirm." This special issue follows in their footsteps, reinterrogating their contributions to SME research without, however, leading to an in-depth exploration of their most reduced segment, particularly SMEs. Beyond the size effect, can SMEs be distinguished from SMEs by their nature?

If we move away from the purely dimensional question, SMEs appear as singular organizational forms, capable of functioning in environments marked by uncertainty. Their light structuring, the high intensity of interactions they mobilize daily, and their proximity to their local ecosystem give them rapid and often innovative adjustment modes. They do not merely reproduce the SME model in miniature: they develop specific ways of coping with constraints, managing resources and envisioning the future, giving rise to original entrepreneurial dynamics, sometimes more sober, more resilient or more iterative than those observed in more established organizations.

Their theoretical discretion contrasts with their statistical and social reality: enterprises with fewer than 10 employees represent more than 90% of enterprises in most European economies. They play an essential role in local ecosystems and embody entrepreneurial projects in their own right: their leaders do not aspire to become SME leaders, they choose the SME through strategic will. This specificity invites us to reconsider the SME as an object of study in itself, endowed with organizational logics and a capacity for continuous evolution that merit closer analysis.

Since 2020, several systemic mutations – health crises, ecological disruptions, resource depletion, inflation, rising inequalities, massive digitization – have fundamentally questioned the foundations of the dominant socio-economic model that tends towards productivity and competitiveness. In this context of chronic instability, SMEs appear as a central heuristic object for thinking differently about the enterprise from an economic, social and even societal point of view. Far from being simple "small enterprises," they constitute a place of experimentation for new models, to be differentiated from models focused on growth or rationalization of processes. Halfway between the micro-entrepreneur and SMEs, does it not prefigure an (or) SME-ist model(s) in its own right?

New forms of projects are developing, oriented towards chosen subsistence, societal contribution, or the search for ethical coherence. These forms are driven by post-materialist aspirations: creating an activity to live differently, to anchor oneself in a territory, to make society differently.

From a socio-economic point of view, the relationship to performance is being reconfigured. For many SMEs, it is no longer a matter of growing at all costs, but of aiming for balance, sustainability, or local impact. Performance becomes multiform: relational, ecological, existential. This choice reflects not opposition to a model, but rather an aspiration to flourish in a proxemic activity, in the space that surrounds the individual, "within reach" (here, of the manager).

The scarcity of resources, no longer perceived as a constraint, becomes a source of innovative strategic behaviors. SMEs engage in processes of resourcefulness, combining frugality, bricolage, mutualization, and reasoned resource management. In a world facing the depletion of natural resources, their ability to make do with little, to invent bold solutions, becomes a strategic competence, even a source of inspiration for other economic models.

The social aspect guides the action of SMEs: the link to material constraint is not limited to economics. From a perspective involving cooperative logics and social and solidarity economy, some SMEs reconfigure their action through a renewed relationship with the living. They integrate natural ecosystems into their governance, relying on participatory and territorialized organizational modes, characteristics of cooperative dynamics. This repositioning leads to practices sometimes informal, but profoundly innovative, that put tension on classical categories of performance and innovation, while reaffirming the role of the enterprise in the preservation and care of environments.

Societal developments, and more specifically the massive arrival of new technologies – digital platforms, automation, AI – profoundly transform the conditions of existence of SMEs, which occupy a particular position between individual entrepreneurship and structured SMEs, that is, organizations that are both very small, flexible, but subject to growing professional and economic demands. Some seize these technologies to create new forms of activity; others are fragile due to processes of uberization and algorithmic dependency; still others develop thanks to the emergence of new needs related to digitization. These transformations also raise social, ethical and political issues concerning the future of self-employment, digital sovereignty and control of tools.

From a micro-economic point of view, the profound renewal of leadership figures: post-salaried career changes, women entrepreneurs, neo-rural residents, young graduates seeking meaning, engaged entrepreneurs. This diversity produces new forms of relationship to work, to growth, and to risk, which merit specific attention. They do not hesitate to question the performance criteria that sit at the center of managerial concerns.

From a meso-economic point of view, the SME is not merely inserted into a local environment: it participates fully in the configuration and evolution of the territorial entrepreneurial system. If some work on entrepreneurial ecosystems has proposed relatively disembodied models, sometimes disconnected from concrete socio-territorial anchors, recent research instead invites us to reaffirm the territorial depth of these dynamics. In the lineage of local productive systems and industrial districts developed by the Italian school, the territory must be understood not as a simple physical support, but as a socio-economic space endowed with identities, resources and specific practices that shape entrepreneurial trajectories. This perspective aligns with the conclusions of the Terram Institute report (2024), according to which SMEs structure the vitality and cohesion of territories. Yet this finding reveals a paradox: dependent on social resources and local networks, they simultaneously contribute to transforming them. Therefore, how can we understand their impact when they are both shaped by the territory and actors in its recomposition?

In total, SMEs can no longer be thought of as reduced versions of SMEs, but as original and pertinent forms of organizations, adapted to an era marked by complexity, uncertainty and planetary limits. They constitute laboratories of resilience, sobriety and entrepreneurial reinvention, often ignored by classical analytical frameworks. They express the essence of robustness, characterized by a high density of interactions. This dynamic creates fertile ground for the development of a continuous evolution capability.

Potential topics

  • Atypical strategic trajectories and diversification of SME leader profiles: profiles, motivations, relationship to work and risk, career bifurcations
  • Redefining performance in SMEs: alternative indicators, rejection of growth, work-life balance, territorial anchoring, relationship to living systems

item.title: Reimagining Accounting for Inclusive Capitalism
item.content:encoded:
Charl de Villiers, University of Auckland

Ruth Dimes, The Open University

Anwar Halari, The Open University

Matteo Molinari, University of Bergamo

Capitalism remains the dominant framework for organising global economic life, yet its promises of prosperity and inclusion have increasingly come under scrutiny. Over the past few decades, the richest 1% have captured more than half of global wealth, while environmental degradation has accelerated at an alarming rate, threatening planetary boundaries. These outcomes have prompted growing calls for more inclusive and sustainable forms of capitalism, leading to the emergence of the concept of Inclusive Capitalism. Inclusive Capitalism seeks to reconcile profit-making with broader societal goals such as environmental stewardship, social justice and economic inclusion. However, its very emergence implies a failure of traditional neoliberal capitalism to deliver on its promises of inclusivity and prosperity. The push for Inclusive Capitalism thus reflects a growing recognition of capitalism's contradictions and the need to rethink how value is defined, measured and distributed.

Accounting is central to this rethinking, as it plays a central role in shaping capitalist systems. Financial accounting information serves as the backbone of capital markets, providing standardised, timely data that investors and other stakeholders rely on to evaluate firm performance and risk, and ultimately to determine share prices. Accounting defines what counts, what gets measured and what gets valued, and in doing so, it legitimises organisational behaviour. However, far from being a neutral technical practice, accounting reflects and reproduces the logics of capitalism. It privileges financial capital while marginalising other forms of value such as social, human, intellectual and natural capitals. Accounting practices are deeply embedded in power structures, legitimising the interests of some while silencing the interests of others.

Critical accounting scholarship has highlighted how accounting can both reproduce and challenge dominant logics and has attempted to theorise how the deep-seated structures underpinning accounting practices work. Scholars and practitioners have sought to imagine how accounting might steer capitalism to more inclusive ends. Developments such as ESG investing, impact investing, stakeholder capitalism, B-Corps and Circular Economy models offer new spaces for reimagining the role of accounting and accountants. More radical approaches such as counter-accounting initiatives and dialogic approaches have promoted participatory and inclusive forms of accountability through challenging capitalism's core logic. These initiatives highlight both the potential and limitations of accounting in supporting alternative forms of capitalism in an increasingly uncertain and polarised world.

This Special Issue invites contributions that critically and constructively examine how accounting may contribute to reimagining capitalism for a more inclusive future. We welcome interdisciplinary perspectives from accounting, finance, economics, law, sociology, political theory, linguistics, history, media studies, and natural sciences. Submissions may adopt critical, interpretive, or mainstream approaches, and may be theoretical, empirical, conceptual, or methodological in nature.

Potential topics

  • Historical and Conceptual Foundations: How has capitalism been historically conceptualised and what role has accounting played in shaping the boundaries of inclusion and exclusion in capitalist systems?
  • Accounting and the Language of Inclusion: How is capitalism linguistically constructed in corporate reports, policy documents, and the media? Why and how has the term 'capital' become associated more with financial capital than other forms of capital (natural, social, human, intellectual) and what are the implications of this? How do metaphors and anthropomorphic representations influence perceptions of accounting's role?
  • Accounting and Technology: How are emerging technologies shaping accounting practices that either widen or narrow inclusion? How might they entrench exclusion, concentrate power, or reinforce surveillance logics within capitalist systems? How is capitalism represented and contested in digital platforms and social media?
  • Critical Perspectives: How do accounting practices reflect and reproduce capitalist logics? What are the tensions between accountability, transparency, and inclusion in capitalist enterprises? Can alternative frameworks (e.g., feminist, indigenous, or social accounting) challenge dominant paradigms?
  • Institutional and Policy Dimensions: How can governments, regulators, and standard-setters use accounting to promote more inclusive and responsible capitalism? What are the implications of developments such as integrated reporting, sustainability standards, and ESG metrics?
  • Religion, Culture and Norms: How do religious organisations, cultural traditions and societal norms shape accounting practices and in what way do these practices create pathways that can support financial and social inclusion, or, conversely, undermine such goals?
  • Management Accounting Practices: How can management accounting systems incorporate multi-capital perspectives? What role do incentive structures and performance measurement play? How do managers change the way they think and act to reflect more integrated and inclusive ways of thinking about value creation?

item.title: Building Digital Capabilities for Improved ESG Performance of Entrepreneurial Firms: Strategies for Tackling Challenges and Capitalizing on Opportunities
item.content:encoded:
Stefano Bresciani, University of Torino

Jawad Abbas, James Cook University

Fauzia Jabeen, Abu Dhabi University

In today's dynamic evolving technology landscape, firms face a transformative wave caused by technological advancements which are omnipresent, from automating manufacturing processes to leveraging big data analytics for strategic decisions. This development warrants entrepreneurial firms to develop digital capabilities strategically to navigate these changes, effectively positioning themselves for innovation and growth and enabling them to improve their Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) performance.

This call for papers focuses on exploring the strategies employed by entrepreneurial firms in building digital capabilities to enhance their ESG performance, addressing challenges, and leveraging opportunities in sustainable business practices.

In an ever-changing technological milieu where technological proficiency is synonymous with competitive advantage, fostering digital capabilities becomes a survival necessity, empowering firms to orchestrate agility, resilience, and sustainable performance. The digital age has ushered in transformative opportunities and challenges, redefining the landscape for entrepreneurial firms striving to align with ethical, social, and environmental responsibilities.

As mentioned in the aims and scope of the International Entrepreneurship and Management Journal, entrepreneurial ventures, characterized by innovation, agility, and risk-taking, are at the forefront of shaping the future of business. Their unique characteristics make them prime actors in navigating the complexities of integrating digital capabilities for improved ESG outcomes. Improving ESG performance is imperative for organizations, transcending mere compliance to embody a commitment to sustainable and ethical practices. This commitment holds profound implications for various stakeholders, ranging from shareholders to customers, suppliers, employees, and others. Improved ESG performance mitigates risks associated with environmental impact and social responsibility, enhances corporate reputation, and attracts conscientious investors. Stakeholders increasingly scrutinize ESG metrics as a reflection of an organization's ethical standing and long-term viability. It fosters a symbiotic relationship, aligning corporate objectives with societal expectations and contributing to building a more responsible and resilient business ecosystem.

This Collection aims to unravel the intricate role of building digital capabilities in entrepreneurial firms' improved ESG performance. By exploring this intersection, we seek to understand how digital capabilities can contribute to a more environmentally and socially responsible entrepreneurial firm with a strong governance structure. We invite experimental, conceptual, theoretical, and empirical studies exploring the convergence of digital capabilities in shaping entrepreneurial firms' ESG performance, shed light on challenges, and explain solutions.

While these topics and questions are our primary interests, we remain open to manuscripts that explain other complexities relevant to digital capabilities and ESG performance. We are keen to receive manuscripts that employ innovative methods and engage deeply with the prevailing dilemmas and dialogues in entrepreneurial research. Your insights and academic rigor will help broaden our collective comprehension of the complexities, challenges, and impacts surrounding building digital capabilities strategies and their implications for ESG performance.

Potential topics

  • How do entrepreneurial ventures define and measure ESG performance in the digital era? And what critical digital capabilities contribute to their improved ESG performance?
  • What challenges do entrepreneurial firms face in integrating digital solutions to enhance environmental sustainability? What could be the best practices for tackling those challenges?
  • What are the possible learning mechanisms and knowledge-sharing processes within entrepreneurial ecosystems that could foster development of digital capabilities for ESG goals?
  • What roles do leadership and organizational culture play in fostering digital capabilities for superior ESG performance in entrepreneurial firms?
  • How can entrepreneurial firms effectively utilize digital technologies to measure and improve their environmental performance within ESG frameworks?
  • How can digital capabilities be harnessed to address diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) challenges in entrepreneurial firms, contributing to improved social sustainability?
  • How do digitalization efforts impact the governance structures of entrepreneurial firms in the context of sustainability? What actions could be taken to improve it?
  • To what extent do regulatory frameworks influence the adoption of digital strategies for ESG compliance in entrepreneurial settings?
  • How do digital technologies facilitate transparency and accountability in ESG reporting for entrepreneurial firms?
  • How can entrepreneurial firms balance profitability goals with sustainable practices through digital transformations? Under this scenario, which opportunities and challenges could arise?
  • What lessons can we learn from recent, real-world cases that showcase the impact of digital capabilities on ESG performance in different industries, particularly entrepreneurial firms, and how can new guidelines lead toward improved ESG performance?

item.title: Digitalization for responsive and circular supply chains
item.content:encoded:
Günter Prockl, Copenhagen Business School

Alexander Pflaum, University of Bamberg

Haozhe Chen, Iowa State University

Marcel Papert, University of Bamberg

The economic environment in which companies create value today is characterized by greater vulnerability, uncertainty, complexity and ambiguity than ever before. Natural disasters, geopolitical conflicts and other disruptions are affecting global supply chains and presenting great changes to established supply chain management models, processes and tools. In the meantime, Planet Earth has reached its limits; climate change and shortages of raw materials are forcing companies and supply chains to transition to more sustainable operations. The commoditization of high-tech products, which is evident in many sectors, is driving the servitization of the manufacturing industry. This presents a golden opportunity for companies to cope with the above-mentioned challenges with greater responsiveness and sustainability.

Tomorrow's supply chains must be able to react quickly to disruptions and changes. The concepts of resilience and responsiveness are key, as are flexibility, agility, adaptability and improvisation. The renewed battle for natural resources requires economic growth to be decoupled from the extraction of raw materials, ultimately forcing a transformation of established 'take, make, waste' supply chains into circular systems. R-strategies such as reduce, reuse, remanufacture and recycle play a special role in doing so. The ultimate aim is to increase resource efficiency in existing value chains, extend the service life of products, and close the loop.

Scientific literature agrees that digital technologies are key to realizing the responsive, servitized and circular supply chains of tomorrow. Important building blocks include the internet of things, artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning, digital twins for products and supply chains, blockchains and digital platforms. However, insufficient research has been conducted into how these building blocks support responsiveness, servitization and the transition to sustainability and circularity as a triple transformation.

This Special Issue seeks contributions that exemplify technology- or data-driven solutions for implementing resilient and circular supply chains, as well as the associated business models. Contributions employing a broad range of methodological approaches are encouraged, including but not limited to conceptual, qualitative, and quantitative research. It is essential that these contributions also derive and discuss managerial implications. We also welcome contributions addressing related topics not listed above.

Contributions should explore digital technologies in supply chain management within today's challenging business environment or specific industry contexts, such as automotive, chemicals, food, life sciences and healthcare, logistics service providers, manufacturing, or mining. Particularly interested are contributions that address the challenges and opportunities associated with digitalization, servitization and transition to sustainability and circularity across multiple supply chain tiers or at least in dyadic relationships.

All papers will be peer reviewed and should conform to Electronic Markets publication standards. Electronic Markets is a SSCI-listed journal with a 2024 Impact Factor of 6.8 and a 5-year Impact Factor of 10.0. Electronic Markets welcomes research from a technological, organizational, societal, and/or political perspective. Since Electronic Markets is a methodologically pluralistic journal, quantitative and qualitative research methods are both welcome as long as the studies are methodologically sound. Conceptual and theory-development papers, empirical hypothesis testing, and case-based studies are all welcome.

item.title: Sustainable Luxury Tourism: Opportunities, Tensions, and Impacts
item.content:encoded:
Kalliopi Chatzipanagiotou, University of Glasgow

Achilleas Boukis, University of Birmingham

George Christodoulides, American University of Sharjah

Raffaele Filieri, Audencia Business School

Luxury tourism is expected to grow faster than any other industry segment. Although scholarship on luxury tourism has expanded in recent years, much of this work focuses on its economic dimensions, often overlooking its broader sustainable, social and ethical implications. The relationship between sustainability and luxury tourism has received increasing attention in recent years, yet we know little about what "sustainable luxury" actually means, given the tension between exclusivity and responsible resource use. Furthermore, while many luxury tourists express concern for sustainability, there remains limited empirical evidence on how such concerns translate into actual decision-making or on the trade-offs they are willing to accept.

At the same time, the experiences of local communities and workers are largely overlooked, pointing to a broader gap around social inequality. Much of the discussion remains focused on minimizing environmental harm, with less attention given to how luxury tourism might actively support more regenerative and inclusive forms of sustainable development. Luxury tourism and hospitality can amplify inequalities, concentrating wealth and privilege within exclusive enclaves while placing disproportionate burdens on local communities, ecosystems, and labour. These tensions between luxury value and impact raise critical questions about who benefits from luxury tourism, who is excluded, and how its growth reshapes societal dynamics, cultural authenticity, and environmental sustainability.

Technological innovation adds further complexity. Artificial intelligence, virtual and augmented reality, and other immersive tools are transforming how sustainable luxury is produced, mediated, and consumed. These technologies may democratize access and enhance personalization, yet they also raise concerns about authenticity, cultural representation, and digital exclusion. Finally, there is a lack of robust methods for assessing the real environmental and social impacts of luxury tourism, while questions about the role of technology are only starting to surface, particularly concerning its environmental footprint and issues of access and inequality.

This Special Issue aims to advance knowledge and debate on sustainable luxury tourism by inviting research that explores how it is defined, experienced, and measured in today's global environment and across various contexts. We also encourage studies of emerging forms of luxury travel, including wellness, medical, and experiential travel, which bring to the fore new environmental concerns and tensions such as the commodification of care and inequalities in access to health and well-being. Finally, this special issue aims to advance our understanding of the tensions inherent in luxury tourism by examining both its aspirational appeal and its darker sides, including environmental degradation, overtourism, cultural appropriation, and labor exploitation. Research on sustainable luxury tourism, whether theoretical, conceptual, or empirical, is encouraged, particularly those that adopt holistic approaches and connect sustainable luxury theory with practical applications. Mixed-method and multi-method submissions are welcomed. Studies focusing on more than one country and culture, as well as those with a longitudinal approach, will be prioritized.

item.title: A Decade (2015-2025) of the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs): Trends, Reflections, and Realignments in Hospitality and Tourism Research
item.content:encoded:
Edmund Goh, Les Roches Abu Dhabi Hospitality Academy

Jun Wen, Macau University of Science and Technology

Siamak Seyfi, University of Oulu

C. Michael Hall, Massey University

Xin-Jean Lim, Sun Yat-Sen University

September 2025 marked the 10th anniversary of the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), a global blueprint for achieving peace, prosperity, and planetary wellbeing. Over the past decade, the hospitality and tourism industries and destination communities have emerged as powerful platforms for advancing and contesting these goals. Hospitality and tourism encompass all 17 SDGs, either directly or indirectly, from economic growth and decent work (SDG 8) to responsible consumption and production (SDG 12), climate action (SDG 13), and partnerships for the goals (SDG 17).

In hospitality and tourism research, SDG 8 (Decent Work and Economic Growth) has guided studies on workforce inclusion, ethical employment, and skills development; SDG 12 (Responsible Consumption and Production) has inspired frameworks for food-waste reduction, sustainable procurement, and circular-economy innovation; and SDG 11 (Sustainable Cities and Communities) has informed investigations into heritage protection, destination resilience, and overtourism management. At the same time, SDG 5 (Gender Equality) and SDG 10 (Reduced Inequalities) have underpinned studies on women's empowerment, migrant labour, and social inclusion across tourism enterprises. Research has also expanded around SDG 13 (Climate Action) and SDG 14/15 (Life Below Water and Life on Land), addressing carbon measurement, biodiversity conservation, and regenerative destination practices.

While studies have advocated that tourism and hospitality can positively contribute to the fulfilment of the UN's ambitious 2030 Agenda, there remains a noticeable gap in how the SDGs are explicitly integrated within scholarly research. Many studies have investigated sustainability-related themes without explicitly aligning their objectives, frameworks, or findings to specific SDG targets, often downplaying or omitting the SDG lens altogether. This disconnect limits the sector's ability to evaluate progress, benchmark impact, and influence policymaking.

This Special Issue responds to those calls by encouraging tourism and hospitality researchers to explicitly reconnect their work to the SDG framework, to identify future research pathways, and to assist policymakers in addressing global challenges through evidence-based strategies. In particular, we seek contributions that illuminate the dynamic linkages between key stakeholders such as hosts, tourists, destinations, government, and industry to explore how these interrelationships can generate more sustainable and equitable outcomes.

This Special Issue seeks to critically assess the progress, limitations, and future directions of SDG-related initiatives in hospitality and tourism. We invite empirical, conceptual, and review papers that evaluate how far the sector has come but also envision pathways for a regenerative, inclusive, and just hospitality and tourism future beyond 2030.

Potential topics

  • Reflecting on the First Decade (2015–2025) of SDG achievements and gaps
  • Critical reviews of how research to date references SDGs and where conceptual or methodological gaps persist
  • Evaluating tourism and hospitality's contribution to all 17 SDGs, including SDG 1 (No Poverty) and SDG 2 (Zero Hunger) through community tourism, local sourcing, and food redistribution
  • Examining progress toward SDG 3 (Good Health and Wellbeing) through wellness tourism, workplace health initiatives, and traveller safety
  • Assessing SDG 4 (Quality Education) via tourism and hospitality curriculum transformation, sustainability literacy, and lifelong learning
  • Policy coherence and alignment of tourism strategies with SDG 16 (Peace, Justice, and Strong Institutions), focusing on governance, transparency, and ethical practices
  • Reviewing the role of SDG 9 (Industry, Innovation, and Infrastructure) in sustainable destination design, transport systems, and smart tourism
  • Integrating SDG 8 (Decent Work), SDG 5 (Gender Equality), and SDG 10 (Reduced Inequalities) through inclusive recruitment, fair wages, and leadership opportunities
  • Advancing SDG 12 (Responsible Consumption and Production) via food waste management, circular hospitality systems, and sustainable event management
  • Strengthening SDG 11 (Sustainable Cities and Communities) by aligning urban tourism, heritage conservation, and destination capacity management
  • Building SDG 17 (Partnerships for the Goals) through cross-sector collaborations among government, academia, and private enterprises

item.title: Innovations in Production Planning: Emerging Problems and Modern Solution Paradigms
item.content:encoded:
Mirco Peron, NEOMA Business School

Ibrahim Kucukkoc, Balikesir University

Daniel Alejandro Rossit, Universidad Nacional del Sur

Ilkyeong Moon, Seoul National University

Olga Battaïa, KEDGE Business School

Michael Pinedo, New York University

Production planning has historically been a central pillar of industrial engineering and operations management. Since the mid-20th century, the field has developed a rich body of classical problems and models, such as lot sizing, job shop and flow shop scheduling, capacity planning, assembly line balancing, material requirements planning (MRP), and aggregate production planning. These models provided structured ways to allocate resources, balance supply and demand, and coordinate activities across production systems, often under deterministic assumptions and with objectives focused primarily on cost and efficiency. Linear programming, dynamic programming, and combinatorial optimization offered rigorous formulations and exact methods, while heuristics and metaheuristics emerged to address large-scale and computationally complex instances.

Over time, production planning research progressively expanded to address uncertainty via stochastic and robust optimization, multi-objective trade-offs (e.g. cost, service level, inventory, lead times), and integration across planning levels (strategic, tactical, and operational). Still, the focus remained on well-defined, structured problems and a relatively stable industrial context.

Today, however, technological, environmental, and societal shifts are reshaping the landscape of production planning. The rise of cyber-physical systems, IoT-enabled factories, advanced robotics, digital twins, additive manufacturing, and AI-based automation has disrupted the stability of traditional assumptions. These innovations have created new types of planning problems, characterized by more frequent reconfiguration, increased heterogeneity of resources, and the necessity of integrating multiple technologies and objectives.

Digital twin–driven planning enables real-time updates of plans and schedules, requiring adaptive and rolling-horizon optimization. Hybrid production systems, combining conventional and additive manufacturing, pose new challenges in sequencing, capacity allocation, and cross-technology coordination. Reconfigurable and modular manufacturing requires planning models that adapt to changing system topologies, dynamic routing, and flexible resource reassignments. Circular and sustainable production systems demand that environmental and social objectives be embedded in planning alongside economic goals. Resilience-oriented planning has become critical in the face of global disruptions, pandemics, and supply shocks, demanding strategies that balance efficiency with adaptability and robustness.

At the same time, innovation has not only transformed the problems but also the solution approaches. Whereas traditional production planning was dominated by mathematical programming and rule-based heuristics, the current era witnesses the rapid adoption of data-driven, hybrid, and AI-enabled methods.

Reinforcement learning and deep learning models are increasingly applied to dynamic planning and scheduling, such as graph neural network and RL architectures for scheduling problems. Hybrid metaheuristics combine classical optimization with machine learning models, surrogate functions, or decomposition techniques to tackle high-dimensional problems. Simulation–optimization coupling allows planners to test, validate, and adapt decisions under complex system dynamics, particularly in systems where analytical modeling is intractable. Multi-agent and distributed approaches enable decentralized planning in highly connected production networks, where local agents coordinate planning decisions. Online and rolling-horizon algorithms become critical when plans must be revised frequently, and incremental updating is required.

Despite these advances, major challenges persist. Industrial adoption demands bridging the gap between academic models and real-world constraints: data sparsity, computational scalability, integration with legacy systems (ERP/MES), and user trust. Decision-makers must also reconcile conflicting objectives: efficiency vs. resilience, speed vs. sustainability, optimality vs. interpretability.

This special issue seeks to collect innovative contributions that redefine the boundaries of production planning. We welcome papers that introduce novel problem formulations reflecting new industrial realities and innovative solution approaches leveraging modern computational, AI, and optimization tools. Both theoretical/methodological and empirical/applied submissions are encouraged, including case studies and empirical validation.

Potential topics

  • Evolution of classical planning problems (lot sizing, capacity planning, scheduling, assembly line balancing) in modern manufacturing contexts
  • Planning in reconfigurable, modular, and hybrid manufacturing systems
  • Integration of additive manufacturing and conventional processes in planning
  • Additive manufacturing production scheduling
  • Digital twin–enabled planning and real-time adaptive scheduling
  • Production planning under sustainability, circular economy, emissions or carbon goals
  • Resilience-oriented planning under uncertainty, disruptions, and volatility
  • Advanced optimization methods: decomposition, robust/stochastic models, metaheuristics
  • Machine learning, reinforcement learning, hybrid AI–optimization for planning
  • Simulation–optimization frameworks and surrogate modeling
  • Production Planning problems associated with customized environments (engineering-to-order, make-to-order, mass customization)
  • Human–robot collaborative systems and operator-driven planning in the context of Industry 5.0
  • Reinforcement learning / deep learning models applied to dynamic planning and scheduling, (e.g., graph neural network and RL architectures for scheduling problems)
  • Optimization of production and inventory strategies in modern distribution systems (e.g., e-commerce, platform-based logistics)
